overview.what_it_is: This lesson builds strong skills with large whole numbers. You will read, round, multiply, divide, and solve problems.

format_facts.label: Main skills
format_facts.value: Place value, rounding, estimating, multiplying, and dividing

format_facts.label: Problem model
format_facts.value: Use bar models to show known and unknown amounts

scoring_factors.name: Place-value accuracy
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each digit has the correct value

scoring_factors.name: Correct method
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the right steps and operations are used

scoring_factors.name: Accurate working
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether every written calculation is correct

scoring_factors.name: Reasonable answer
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether an estimate supports the final answer

critical_rules: A digit changes value when its place changes.
For rounding, look one place to the right.
A right-hand digit of five or more rounds up.
Multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction.
Do multiplication and division from left to right.
State the answer with the correct unit or label.

learning_goals: You will read numbers up to the millions.
You will write large numbers in words and figures.
You will find the value of any digit.
You will round to tens, hundreds, and thousands.
You will use estimates to check exact answers.
You will multiply and divide using place value.
You will follow the correct order of operations.
You will solve word problems using bar models.

core_method.name: Read → Choose → Model → Work → Check → Answer
core_method.summary: Read the number carefully. Choose the skill. Show each step. Check whether the answer makes sense.

steps.detail: Find the important digits, words, and number places.
Choose place value, rounding, or an operation.
Use a place chart or bar model when helpful.
Show each calculation in the correct order.
Use place value, inverse operations, or an estimate.
Write a clear sentence with the correct unit.

techniques.name: Build a place-value chart
techniques.purpose: Shows the value held by each digit.
how_to: Draw columns from ones to millions.
Write one digit inside each correct column.
Find the column holding the chosen digit.
Write the digit times its place value.
techniques.example: In $72{,}845$, the digit $8$ is in the hundreds place. Its value is $8 \times 100 = 800$.
techniques.why_it_matters: It stops digits from being read in the wrong place.
techniques.common_error: Calling the digit itself its value, such as saying $8$.

techniques.name: Read numbers in three-digit groups
techniques.purpose: Makes large numbers easier to read and write.
how_to: Split the number into groups of three digits.
Read the left group first.
Say million or thousand after its group.
Read the last group without adding a group name.
techniques.example: $435{,}672$ becomes $435$ thousand and $672$. It is four hundred thirty-five thousand, six hundred seventy-two.
techniques.why_it_matters: Three-digit groups keep number names in the correct order.
techniques.common_error: Skipping a place that contains zero.

techniques.name: Use the rounding neighbour
techniques.purpose: Finds the closest ten, hundred, or thousand.
how_to: Find the place being rounded.
Look one digit to its right.
Keep the place if that digit is below five.
Raise the place by one if it is five or more.
Change all digits to the right into zeros.
techniques.example: For $4{,}865$ to the nearest hundred, look at $6$. Since $6 \geq 5$, $4{,}865 \approx 4{,}900$.
techniques.why_it_matters: Only one nearby digit decides the rounding direction.
techniques.common_error: Looking at every digit to the right.

techniques.name: Estimate with friendly numbers
techniques.purpose: Gives a quick answer for checking exact work.
how_to: Round each number to a nearby friendly number.
Keep the rounded numbers close to the originals.
Work out the easier calculation.
Compare the estimate with the exact answer.
techniques.why_it_matters: A very different exact answer may show an error.
techniques.common_error: Rounding so much that the estimate becomes unhelpful.

techniques.name: Shift places when multiplying
techniques.purpose: Uses place value for tens, hundreds, and thousands.
how_to: Find how many zeros are in the multiplier.
Move every digit left by that many places.
Use zero as a place holder when needed.
Read the result using the place-value chart.
techniques.example: $43 \times 100 = 4{,}300$ because each digit moves two places left.
techniques.why_it_matters: It explains why the number becomes ten times larger.
techniques.common_error: Adding zeros without thinking about each digit.

techniques.name: Break apart a multiple of ten
techniques.purpose: Makes multiplication and division easier to manage.
how_to: Split the number into a basic fact and ten.
Complete the basic multiplication or division.
Complete the remaining factor of ten.
Check using the inverse operation.
techniques.why_it_matters: Known number facts can solve larger calculations.
techniques.common_error: Forgetting the final factor of ten.

techniques.name: Follow operation priority
techniques.purpose: Keeps mixed calculations in the correct order.
how_to: Look for multiplication and division first.
Work from left to right between equal operations.
Then complete addition and subtraction.
Check each line before moving forward.
techniques.why_it_matters: Changing the order can change the answer.
techniques.common_error: Working only from left to right.

techniques.name: Draw a bar model
techniques.purpose: Shows the parts and the unknown amount.
how_to: Draw one bar for the whole amount.
Split the bar into equal or known parts.
Label every amount from the question.
Mark the missing part with a question mark.
Choose operations that match the bar.
techniques.example: For profit, show sales as the whole bar. Split it into cost and profit.
techniques.why_it_matters: The picture shows which operation should be used.
techniques.common_error: Choosing an operation before understanding the story.

worked_examples.title: Read a number and find a digit value
worked_examples.input: Write $435{,}672$ in words. Find the value of $5$.
worked_examples.decoding: Split the number into $435$ thousand and $672$. The digit $5$ is in the thousands place.
worked_examples.plan: Read each three-digit group. Then multiply $5$ by its place.
worked_examples.model_answer: First split the number: $435{,}672 = 435{,}000 + 672$. Read the first group as four hundred thirty-five thousand. Read the last group as six hundred seventy-two. The full number is four hundred thirty-five thousand, six hundred seventy-two. The digit $5$ is in the thousands place. Its value is $5 \times 1{,}000 = 5{,}000$. Therefore, the value of $5$ is $5{,}000$.

annotations.comment: This separates the thousands group from the last group.
The word thousand belongs after the first group.
The last group does not need another group name.
The multiplication shows the full value of the digit.

worked_examples.title: Round and estimate a product
worked_examples.input: Round $4{,}865$ to the nearest hundred. Estimate $702 \times 19$.
worked_examples.decoding: The first task needs the tens digit. The second task needs friendly nearby numbers.
worked_examples.plan: Use $6$ to round the first number. Round the factors before multiplying.
worked_examples.model_answer: For $4{,}865$, the hundreds digit is $8$. The digit to its right is $6$. Since $6 \geq 5$, raise the hundreds digit by one. So, $4{,}865 \approx 4{,}900$. For the product, round $702$ to $700$. Round $19$ to $20$. Then $702 \times 19 \approx 700 \times 20 = 14{,}000$. The estimated product is $14{,}000$.

annotations.part: the digit to its right is $6$
annotations.comment: The tens digit decides the nearest hundred.
Five or more means the rounding place increases.
This keeps the rounded number close to the original.
Twenty makes the multiplication quick.
This is the estimate, not the exact product.

worked_examples.title: Multiply and divide using tens
worked_examples.decoding: Both calculations contain a multiple of ten. Break each one into smaller factors.
worked_examples.model_answer: First work out $16 \times 70$. Break $70$ into $7 \times 10$. Then $16 \times 70 = 16 \times 7 \times 10$. Work out $16 \times 7 = 112$. Then $112 \times 10 = 1{,}120$. So, $16 \times 70 = 1{,}120$. Next work out $15{,}000 \div 30$. Break $30$ into $10 \times 3$. Then $15{,}000 \div 30 = 15{,}000 \div 10 \div 3$. Work out $15{,}000 \div 10 = 1{,}500$. Then $1{,}500 \div 3 = 500$. Therefore, $15{,}000 \div 30 = 500$.

annotations.comment: This turns the problem into two easier multiplications.
Complete the basic fact before multiplying by ten.
This lets the division happen in two steps.
Each digit moves one place right.
This completes the second part of the divisor.

worked_examples.title: Use the correct operation order
worked_examples.decoding: The expression contains addition and multiplication. Multiplication must be completed first.
worked_examples.model_answer: Multiplication comes before addition. First work out $3 \times 6 = 18$. Replace the multiplication part with $18$. Then $9 + 3 \times 6 = 9 + 18$. Finally, $9 + 18 = 27$. Therefore, the value of the expression is $27$.

annotations.comment: The multiplication is completed before the addition.
The multiplication part is replaced by its value.
Addition is completed after multiplication.
This differs from adding the first two numbers first.

worked_examples.title: Find profit from mango sales
worked_examples.input: Alicia has $420$ mangoes. She packs $4$ mangoes in each bag. She sells each bag for $6$. The mangoes cost $378$. Find her profit.
worked_examples.decoding: First find the number of bags. Then find total sales. Profit is sales minus cost.
worked_examples.plan: Use three steps: divide, multiply, then subtract.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model in words: One bar shows all $420$ mangoes. Split it into equal groups of $4$ mangoes. A second bar shows all sales money. Split the sales bar into the cost part and profit part. First find the number of bags: $420 \div 4 = 105$. Alicia has $105$ bags. Next find the sales money: $105 \times 6 = 630$. Alicia receives $630$. Finally find the profit: $630 - 378 = 252$. Therefore, Alicia makes a profit of $252$.

annotations.part: split it into equal groups of $4$ mangoes
annotations.comment: Equal groups show that division is needed.
This finds how many bags Alicia can fill.
This finds the total money from all bags.
Subtracting the cost gives the profit.
The final sentence states the answer and its meaning.

worked_examples.title: Correct a halfway rounding mistake
worked_examples.input: A pupil says $16{,}500$ rounds to $16{,}000$ to the nearest thousand. Correct the mistake.
worked_examples.decoding: The number is halfway between two thousands. The hundreds digit is exactly $5$.
worked_examples.plan: Use the rule that five or more rounds upward.
worked_examples.model_answer: The thousands digit in $16{,}500$ is $6$. The digit to its right is $5$. A right-hand digit of $5$ or more rounds up. Raise the thousands digit from $6$ to $7$. Change the digits to its right into zeros. Therefore, $16{,}500 \approx 17{,}000$ to the nearest thousand. The pupil should round up, not down.

annotations.part: the digit to its right is $5$
annotations.comment: The hundreds digit decides the nearest thousand.
This rule includes numbers exactly halfway.
Only the rounding-place digit increases.
The approximation sign shows this is a rounded value.

items.when_to_use: Use it for one symbol from $0$ to $9$.
Use it for a digit's value in its position.
Use it for the first place from the right.
Use it for a digit worth groups of $1{,}000$.
Use it when choosing the closest target number.
Use it when the next digit is $5$ or more.
Use it when the next digit is below $5$.
Use it for a quick answer near the exact answer.
Use it for the answer to an addition.
Use it for the answer to a subtraction.
Use it for the answer to a multiplication.
Use it for the answer to a division.
Use it for the number being divided.
Use it for the number you divide by.
Use it for the amount left after equal sharing.
Use it when sharing into groups of the same size.
It often tells you to add amounts.
It often asks for the difference.
It often shows equal groups or equal prices.
Use it for sales money minus the cost.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving the digit instead of its full value.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The digit's place may make it worth much more.
common_mistakes.fix: Write the digit times its place value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading large numbers without three-digit groups.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Thousands and millions may be placed incorrectly.
common_mistakes.fix: Split the number into groups from the right.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding down when the next digit is $5$.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Five belongs to the round-up group.
common_mistakes.fix: Use zero to four down, five to nine up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing digits on the left while rounding.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Only the rounding place may increase.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep all places left of it unchanged.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding zeros without using place value.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This rule fails when decimals or place holders appear.
common_mistakes.fix: Think about each digit moving between places.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The answer becomes ten or one hundred times too small.
common_mistakes.fix: Break the number into factors before working.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding before multiplying in a mixed expression.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It changes the value of the expression.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing an operation from one word only.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The story may use that word in another way.
common_mistakes.fix: Draw a bar model and check the whole story.

time_budget.focus: Read numbers and name digit values
Change between figures and written words
Round to tens, hundreds, and thousands
Use friendly numbers before exact work
Use place shifts and factor breaking
Draw bar models and show full working

drills.name: Digit value hunt
drills.instructions: Write six large numbers. Circle one digit. State its value.

drills.name: Words and figures swap
drills.instructions: Write four numbers in words. Change four words into figures.

drills.name: Rounding ladder
drills.instructions: Round six numbers to the nearest ten, hundred, and thousand.

drills.name: Estimate first
drills.instructions: Estimate five products. Then find each exact answer.

drills.name: Place-shift cards
drills.instructions: Multiply and divide number cards by $10$, $100$, and $1{,}000$.

drills.name: Order race
drills.instructions: Solve six mixed expressions. Underline the first operation.

drills.name: Bar-model stories
drills.instructions: Draw a bar model for four short word problems.

drills.name: Explain the error
drills.instructions: Correct four wrong answers. Explain each mistake aloud.

practice_plan.routine: Study one skill at a time. Model one example. Try four questions. Check each answer. Explain one method aloud. Review mistakes before starting the next skill.

mastery_checklist: I can read whole numbers up to the millions.
I can write large numbers using words and figures.
I can state the full value of any digit.
I can use zero as a place holder.
I can round to the nearest ten.
I can round to the nearest hundred.
I can round to the nearest thousand.
I can make useful estimates before exact work.
I can break apart multiples such as $70$ and $300$.
I can follow the correct order of operations.
I can draw a bar model for a word problem.
I can check whether my final answer is reasonable.
strategy_notes: Cover the digits to the right when reading place value.
Mark the rounding place before looking beside it.
Say the rounding rule quietly before changing digits.
Estimate before exact work when numbers are large.
Use inverse operations to check multiplication and division.
Underline multiplication and division in mixed expressions.
Draw the bar model before choosing an operation.
Write one calculation on each clear line.
Keep labels such as dollars, bags, or mangoes.
Correct mistakes by naming the broken rule.
